title: Learning What to Ask for Tomorrow: Active Preference Acquisition for Long-Term Personalized Web Agents

paper.title: Learning What to Ask for Tomorrow: Active Preference Acquisition for Long-Term Personalized Web Agents
paper.abstract:
Abstract. Web agents increasingly serve the same user across repeated online tasks such as booking travel, shopping, and scheduling, so their long-term usefulness depends on how well they know the user’s preferences.
Passive memory and personalization methods cannot obtain preferences the user never reveals, and clarification methods that value a question by its benefit to the current task overlook the benefit of reusing the answer in later tasks.
We study Active Preference Acquisition (APA): which missing preferences are worth the cost of asking?
We define the Prospective Personalization Value (PPV) of a missing preference as its expected cumulative utility gain over future tasks minus the effort and disclosure-risk cost of asking, and select questions under a per-interaction budget. We characterize when cumulative reuse justifies acquisition despite insufficient single-task benefit, and evaluate this regime with an initial-profile diagnostic.
APA computes the counterfactual gain of each candidate preference on public task prototypes with the agent’s own task solver and aggregates it by the expected reuse of each task family. We evaluate it on ActiveWebPref, a controlled longitudinal benchmark with hidden but queryable user profiles and exact task utilities.
At a horizon of 20 tasks, 34.4% of budget-feasible valuable missing preferences are amortization-dependent; APA acquires 80.3% of them, whereas current-task value of information acquires 5.1%.
Under per-user asking-cost caps matched to APA’s realized expenditure, APA achieves higher net utility than random, frequency-based, impact-based and LLM-ranked selection.
In our cost setting, asking about every unknown preference yields lower net utility than not asking, while APA recovers 84.2% of its utility gain with 27.6% of its questions.
The value of acquiring a user preference should account for its reuse across future tasks, not only its benefit to the task at hand.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Web agents can now carry out realistic Web tasks such as online shopping and navigating real-world websites ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Deng et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) , and they are moving from one-shot assistance to persistent service. The same agent may book a user’s conference travel in March, order office supplies in April, and reserve a team dinner in May. Its usefulness over time then depends less on any single task than on how well it knows the user : that the user avoids red-eye flights, keeps hotels under a per-night budget, and needs vegetarian options. This paper studies that user-modeling problem for users of persistent Web agents: which missing preferences a persistent Web agent should acquire, and when doing so pays off. Valuable preferences, however, need not appear in the interaction history. Personalization methods condition on past behavior ( Salemi et al., 2024 ) or infer profiles from what users have said ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and long-term memory systems decide how to extract, store, retrieve, and update observed information ( Packer et al., 2023 ; Zhong et al., 2024 ; Chhikara et al., 2025 ; Rasmussen et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . These methods work with evidence that exists; a preference the user has never had reason to mention or to reveal through behavior cannot be extracted or retrieved. Asking can fill such gaps, but asking is not free: each question costs the user effort, and each answer discloses personal information. An agent therefore cannot simply ask about everything; in our experiments, asking about every unknown preference, or about whatever an LLM deems most worth knowing, yields lower net utility than not asking at all (§ 6 ). Figure 1. A preference that is useless now can be valuable later. In session t t the user asks for a hotel, and the seat preference m m is unknown. For the current task, knowing m m has no value ( V current ​ ( m ) ≈ 0 V_{\text{current}}(m)\approx 0 ), so a clarification agent does not ask. Every later seat selection needs it, so V future ​ ( m ) > 0 V_{\text{future}}(m)>0 ; when this expected cumulative benefit exceeds the one-time cost of asking, acquiring it once and reusing it is worthwhile. Timeline from session t to t+3. In session t the user books a hotel; a missing seat preference has no immediate value. In sessions t+1 to t+3 flight, conference-travel and business-trip bookings each require selecting a seat, so acquiring the preference once and reusing it is valuable. Valuing each question by the current task does not resolve this either. Current-task clarification and value-of-information (VoI) methods ask when a question improves the current task enough to justify its cost ( Rao and Daumé III, 2018 ; Aliannejadi et al., 2019 ; Zamani et al., 2020 ; Dong et al., 2026 ) . While booking a hotel, the agent can finish without the user’s seat preference, so current-task VoI does not ask (Figure 1 ). Why not wait and ask when a flight is booked? Because even then, a single booking’s gain may not cover the cost of asking; only reuse across many later bookings does. A criterion that values a question only by the task at hand then never acquires such a preference, however often it is reused (Proposition 3.1 ). An agent therefore needs to value acquisition across tasks: Which currently unknown user preferences are worth acquiring, because their benefit across future tasks outweighs the cost of asking? We call this problem Active Preference Acquisition (APA). At each interaction the agent holds a partial profile and can already complete the current task; it decides which missing preferences to ask about and stores the answers persistently. Unlike cold-start elicitation or within-session clarification, APA interleaves acquisition with ongoing service and values persistent attributes by their reuse across heterogeneous future tasks. We define the Prospective Personalization Value (PPV) of a missing preference: its expected utility gain across future tasks, minus the effort and disclosure-risk cost of asking. PPV complements clarification rather than generalizing it, and the key distinction is in how a preference is valued, not when it is asked: a cross-task criterion may still ask at the first relevant task. We estimate PPV by counterfactual reuse valuation . For each candidate missing preference, the agent’s own task solver computes how much knowing it would change utility on public task prototypes, and these gains are aggregated by the expected reuse of each task family; questions are then selected under asking cost, disclosure risk and a per-interaction budget. To test when this helps and by how much, we build ActiveWebPref, a controlled longitudinal testbed modeled on personalized Web services, with hidden but queryable user profiles, multi-domain task sequences, and exact task utilities. It isolates the value of preference acquisition, which existing memory benchmarks do not measure ( Wu et al., 2025a ; Maharana et al., 2024 ) , and does not evaluate agents acting on live websites. Contributions. (1) Problem. We formulate Active Preference Acquisition and define PPV. We show that a criterion valuing only the current task never acquires a preference whose benefit on every single task is below the asking cost, however often it is reused, whereas PPV assigns it positive value once cumulative reuse covers that cost (Proposition 3.1 ). (2) Method. APA estimates PPV by counterfactual reuse valuation: the agent’s own task solver computes each candidate’s gain on public task prototypes, weighted by the expected reuse of each task family, and an adaptive greedy policy selects questions under asking cost, disclosure risk and a per-interaction budget (§ 4 ). (3) Benchmark. ActiveWebPref is a controlled longitudinal benchmark with 16 task families, hidden but queryable user profiles and exact task utilities, so the counterfactual value of an unasked preference can be measured; an initial-profile diagnostic identifies amortization-dependent preferences (§ 5 ). Code, data and prompts are available at https://github.com/xiaoqi-7/Active-Preference-Acquisition . (4) Findings. At a horizon of T = 20 T=20 tasks, 34.4% of budget-feasible valuable initially missing preferences are amortization-dependent; APA acquires 80.3% of them and Current-task VoI (public) 5.1%, while the NU-maximizing oracle acquires 44.9%, so the aim is selective rather than maximal acquisition. Among users with at least one such preference, APA improves whole-sequence net utility over Current-task VoI (public) at T = 20 T=20 (Holm p = 0.021 p=0.021 ) but not significantly at T = 10 T=10 . Under per-user asking-cost caps matched to APA’s realized expenditure, APA achieves higher net utility than random, frequency-based, impact-based and LLM-ranked selection (all Holm p ≤ 0.0025 p\leq 0.0025 ). In our cost setting, cost-blind asking yields lower net utility than not asking, while APA recovers 84.2% of exhaustive asking’s utility gain with 27.6% of its questions (§ 6 ).

sections.heading: User modeling and personalization.
sections.text: Personalized systems condition generation or ranking on user profiles, given as explicit persona statements ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) or drawn from behavioral history ( Salemi et al., 2024 ) . Recent LLM agents continuously infer and refine a unified user profile from dialogue turns ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , or update preference memories as user behavior evolves by fusing short- and long-term averages ( Sun et al., 2026 ) . These methods infer preferences from evidence that already exists. They cannot recover a preference that has never been expressed or revealed through behavior, and they do not decide which unobserved preferences are worth eliciting for future tasks.

sections.heading: Preference elicitation.
sections.text: Decision-theoretic preference elicitation frames question asking as a POMDP that trades question cost against the quality of a final decision ( Boutilier, 2002 ) . Recommender systems ask new users to rate items in a cold-start interview ( Rashid et al., 2002 ) , possibly adapting the next item to earlier answers with a decision tree ( Golbandi et al., 2011 ) , and use active learning in collaborative filtering more broadly ( Elahi et al., 2016 ) . Conversational recommenders decide within a session which item or attribute to ask about next ( Christakopoulou et al., 2016 ; Sun and Zhang, 2018 ; Lei et al., 2020a ; Lei et al., 2020b ; Deng et al., 2021 ; Jannach et al., 2021 ) . LLMs have also been used to elicit preferences through open-ended questions: GATE prompts models to elicit a user’s intended task behavior ( Li et al., 2025 ) , and STaR-GATE fine-tunes a questioner to ask useful clarifying questions ( Andukuri et al., 2024 ) . APA differs from this work in three ways. (i) When and why to ask. Conversational elicitation asks in order to finish the current session. Cold-start interviews do ask for future benefit, but in a single onboarding step before any task is served. In APA, questions are interleaved with ongoing tasks that can already be completed, and each question is justified by its expected effect on future tasks. (ii) Scope. Elicitation targets item ratings or attributes within a single catalog. APA acquires persistent user attributes that are reused across heterogeneous task families, such as flights, hotels, dining, and scheduling. (iii) Valuation target. Like prior elicitation, APA weighs benefit against the cost of asking; the difference is that the benefit is counted across the heterogeneous future tasks that reuse the answer, rather than within one decision or session. APA builds on established value-of-information and preference-elicitation principles ( Howard, 1966 ; Boutilier, 2002 ) , operationalizing them for persistent preferences reused across heterogeneous tasks, and adds a benchmark in which the counterfactual value of an unasked preference can be measured.

sections.heading: Long-term memory for agents.
sections.text: Surveys organize agent memory by its sources, forms, and operations (writing, management, and reading) ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) . Memory architectures give LLM agents persistent state through hierarchical context management ( Packer et al., 2023 ) , memory streams with reflection ( Park et al., 2023 ) , forgetting-aware stores ( Zhong et al., 2024 ) , scalable extraction and retrieval ( Chhikara et al., 2025 ) , and temporal knowledge graphs ( Rasmussen et al., 2025 ) . ProMem improves memory extraction itself: it extracts details, events, and relations separately, checks completeness to recover missed events, and verifies atomic facts ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . Benchmarks such as LongMemEval ( Wu et al., 2025a ) and LoCoMo ( Maharana et al., 2024 ) test whether facts present in the history can be recalled. PrefEval tests whether models follow stated or implicit preferences ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) , and PersonaMem whether they track preferences that evolve across sessions ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) ; both find that preferences already expressed are often not followed. These systems answer how to retain and use what is known . APA addresses which unknown information should be learned , and can run on top of any of them.

sections.heading: Clarification and value of information.
sections.text: Asking clarifying questions has been studied in information retrieval ( Aliannejadi et al., 2019 ; Zamani et al., 2020 ) and in NLP, for example by ranking questions by expected value of perfect information ( Rao and Daumé III, 2018 ) . For LLM agents, the IN3 benchmark annotates which details of a vague task are missing, and Mistral-Interact is trained to ask about them before executing ( Qian et al., 2024 ) , and Ask-before-Plan studies clarification before travel planning ( Zhang et al., 2024b ) . Proactive Agent instead anticipates and offers help that the user has not requested ( Lu et al., 2025 ) . Dong et al. ( Dong et al., 2026 ) formalize when an agent should ask rather than act by weighing the expected utility gain of a question on the current decision against the cost it imposes on the user. Two lines of work look beyond the current response: one labels response preferences by simulating future conversation turns, teaching models when to ask clarifying questions ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) , and CollabLLM trains models with a multiturn-aware reward estimated from simulated future conversations ( Wu et al., 2025b ) . Their horizon, however, is later turns of the same conversation, whereas the horizon of APA is future tasks across sessions. Abstracting from these methods, current-task clarification scores a question about m m as V cur ​ ( m ) = Δ ​ U ​ ( τ t , m ) − C ⁡ ( m ) , V_{\text{cur}}(m)=\Delta U(\tau_{t};m)-C(m), whereas APA scores the same preference by its value over the tasks that follow, P ​ P ​ V T ​ ( m ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ ∑ k = t + 1 T Δ ​ U ​ ( τ k , m ) ] − C ⁡ ( m ) . PPV_{T}(m)=\mathbb{E}\Big[\textstyle\sum_{k=t+1}^{T}\Delta U(\tau_{k};m)\Big]-C(m). The two scores answer different questions and are complementary. Howard’s formulation values information for a single decision problem ( Howard, 1966 ) , and the non-myopic VoI of Krause and Guestrin ( Krause and Guestrin, 2005 ) selects a budget-constrained set of observations jointly, rather than greedily, to reduce uncertainty in one fixed model. These principles can accommodate long-term benefit; APA instantiates them as a longitudinal personalization decision. The information is stored, and it pays off across many future tasks drawn from an uncertain task distribution.

sections.heading: Web agents.
sections.text: Benchmarks for Web agents such as WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , Mind2Web ( Deng et al., 2023 ) , and WebArena ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) pose each episode as a single, self-contained instruction, with no user state carried across tasks. Personalized Web agents have recently been studied through PersonalWAB, which pairs simulated users’ profiles and behavior histories with personalized search, recommendation, and review tasks and whose multi-turn track lets the agent clarify a request with a simulated user ( Cai et al., 2025 ) , and Persona2Web, which requires agents on the open Web to resolve ambiguous queries from long user histories ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . Both personalize mainly from histories, and any questions serve the current request. Neither studies which missing preferences an agent should acquire for future tasks.

sections.text: A user u u interacts with an agent over a sequence of tasks τ 1 , … , τ T \tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{T} . Each task belongs to a task family f ⁡ ( τ ) ∈ ℱ f(\tau)\in\mathcal{F} , such as flight booking, hotel selection, restaurant reservation, or meeting scheduling. At step t t the agent observes the interaction history H t H_{t} and maintains a persistent profile P t P_{t} , a set of attribute–value pairs such as ( seat , aisle ) (\textit{seat},\textit{aisle}) . The user has a hidden ground-truth profile P u ∗ P^{*}_{u} , and the agent’s profile is a subset of it, P t ⊆ P u ∗ P_{t}\subseteq P^{*}_{u} . Given a task and a profile, the agent’s task solver selects an action whose utility U ⁡ ( τ ∣ P ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] U(\tau\mid P)\in[0,1] is determined by P u ∗ P^{*}_{u} . In ActiveWebPref, U U is computed exactly from the hidden profile (§ 5 ). Figure 2. Overview of APA. ① Gap discovery proposes preferences 𝒢 t \mathcal{G}_{t} missing from the profile P t P_{t} . ② Future reuse modeling estimates how often each may be reused, from a coarse distribution over task families. ③ Prospective value estimation scores each by relevance and impact. ④ Cost-aware acquisition subtracts asking cost and disclosure risk and chooses Ask , Defer , or Skip . Here, the seat preference is asked; the dining preference, rarely reused because restaurant tasks are rare, is deferred for later re-scoring, as is the hotel budget once the seat question has used this interaction’s budget; and a previously refused political preference, which never enters the candidate set, is skipped. Answers update the profile for future tasks. Four-stage pipeline: gap discovery, future reuse modeling, a relevance-impact matrix for value estimation, and a cost-aware policy that asks about the seat preference, defers the rarely reused dining preference (and the hotel budget once the interaction budget is spent), and skips a previously refused political preference; answers update the persistent profile.

sections.heading: 4. The APA Framework
sections.text: APA estimates the terms of Eq. ( 1 ) with four modules (Figure 2 ). Its core is counterfactual reuse valuation (§ 4.3 ) combined with cost-sensitive budgeted selection (§ 4.4 ); gap discovery (§ 4.1 ) and future reuse modeling (§ 4.2 ) are implementation components that supply candidates and reuse estimates. To isolate the acquisition decision, all LLM roles share the same backbone, and all policies share the same deterministic task solver. Prompts are given in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 4.1. Preference Gap Discovery
sections.text: The agent knows a complete public attribute catalogue but not the user's missing values; it selects which unknown fields to evaluate for acquisition. Given ( H t , P t ) (H_{t},P_{t}) and the arrived task (null before the sequence), a proposer LLM selects min ⁡ ( K , | 𝒜 t | ) \min(K,|\mathcal{A}_{t}|) distinct IDs from the allowed unknown-field set 𝒜 t \mathcal{A}_{t} , predicting stability and a natural-language question q i q_{i} . The catalogue supplies each description, so the resulting candidates retain the form ( m i , description i , stability i , q i ) (m_{i},\text{description}_{i},\text{stability}_{i},q_{i}) . sections.heading: 4.5. Profile Update and Reuse
sections.text: Answers are written as typed attribute–value pairs to a structured persistent profile; user-local permission is updated after success or refusal. Source, step and sensitivity are retained in the experiment logs. Every later task in any domain can read them. In the main comparison, all policies share the same simple profile store, so differences in results come from acquisition alone.

sections.heading: 5. ActiveWebPref and Experimental Setup
sections.text: Existing long-term memory benchmarks either place the information needed for each question in the history or ask models to abstain when it is absent ( Wu et al., 2025a ; Maharana et al., 2024 ) ; none rewards acquiring missing information. APA instead requires preferences that are useful but initially absent from the history . It also requires task utilities that can be computed exactly, so that the benefit of a question can be measured without an LLM judge. We therefore build ActiveWebPref as a controlled longitudinal testbed. The benchmarks discussed in § 2 do not directly provide a protocol with hidden but queryable profiles and counterfactual utilities of unasked preferences. ActiveWebPref is deliberately controlled so that the counterfactual utility of an unasked preference is known exactly, allowing us to measure whether each question was worth asking. This control comes at the cost of realism, which we discuss in § 8 .

sections.heading: Domains and task families.
sections.text: ActiveWebPref covers five service domains: Travel (flight booking, hotel selection, ground transport, conference trips), Dining (restaurant choice, reservation, takeaway), Shopping (product selection, gifts, repeat purchases), Scheduling (meetings, recurring events, appointments), and Work/Conference (conference, coordination, work events): 16 task families in total. Task options are synthetic structured alternatives, rather than items taken from live Web catalogues.

sections.heading: Hidden user profiles.
sections.text: Each synthetic user has 27 attributes. Each attribute has a ground-truth value and the following metadata: • stability : stable, semi-stable, or ephemeral; • sensitivity : low, medium, or high; • a normalized fixed asking cost c m ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] c_{m}\in[0,1] ; • the set of relevant task families ℛ ⁡ ( m ) \mathcal{R}(m) and an impact level; • whether it is initially observed; • whether it is queryable. Between 40% and 60% of useful attributes are hidden at t = 0 t=0 . Profiles are stored separately from dialogues and are visible only to the user simulator and the evaluator. The privileged oracle also accesses the hidden profile; practical policies receive the public catalogue and visible profile/history only.

sections.heading: Task sequences.
sections.text: For each user we save a separate initial context and 20 future tasks. Main CTU evaluates the first T = 10 T=10 future tasks; horizon scaling uses nested prefixes T ∈ { 1 , 3 , 5 , 10 , 20 } T\in\{1,3,5,10,20\} . The generator varies reuse frequency, cross-domain relevance, acquisition cost, sensitivity, and attribute dependence, to evaluate their effects on acquisition decisions. It includes five kinds of attributes: • attributes with heterogeneous reuse: some are used once, some repeatedly, some never; • cross-domain attributes (e.g., meeting mode) as well as domain-specific ones (e.g., seat preference); • distractors : attributes that look personal but never affect utility; • attributes that are high-value but also high-cost or high-sensitivity; • correlated attributes, whose joint value may be less than the sum of their individual values.

sections.heading: Exact utilities and user simulator.
sections.text: As in evaluations that separate user-side private information from the agent ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Balog and Zhai, 2025 ) , each task has a candidate set, for example flight options with seat, layover, and price attributes. The solver picks the best candidate under the agent’s current profile, and utility is the score of that pick under P u ∗ P^{*}_{u} . The simulator answers only questions that map to a single queryable attribute and never reveals other attributes. Requests for non-queryable or high-sensitivity fields are refused, and the refused question still incurs its asking cost. Risk is charged only on successful disclosure. The main experiments use a deterministic structured answer mode.

sections.text: The two disjoint test splits contain IID users and users with unseen preference combinations. All splits were frozen before any test-set evaluation. The train split is not used by any policy, for parameter selection, or for prototype sampling; it is retained as a benchmark split and used to verify that the unseen combinations occur in neither train nor dev. sections.heading: 5.2. Baselines
sections.text: All policies share the task solver, profile store and simulator; every LLM role uses the same backbone. The main table compares the core measured policies; the implementation also includes the simple policies listed below. • Controls. Ask-Nothing uses only the initially observed profile. Ask-Everything asks all unknown publicly eligible fields without a binding budget and pays for every attempted question, including refusals. • Simple policies. Selection obeys the acquisition-cost cap. – Random- k k : random candidates, averaged over 5 seeds. – Frequency : estimated reuse only. – Impact-only : ranks candidates by max f ∈ ℱ ⁡ I ⁡ ( m , f ) \max_{f\in\mathcal{F}}I(m,f) , the largest family-specific counterfactual impact, without reuse weighting or cost/risk penalties in the ranking. – LLM-Importance : the same backbone ranks “which unknown facts are most worth knowing”, without task decomposition. • Current-task VoI ( Dong et al., 2026 ) : an adaptation closer to the LLM-based current-task VoI formulation of Dong et al. (ACL 2026), in which Qwen predicts relative probabilities of unknown preference states for the current task. The shared solver computes the resulting current-task information gain; no future task is used. At the default setting it reaches NU 6.480 (CTU 6.640, AC 0.318, 1.82 questions), below the public-belief version, which we therefore use as the stronger current-task baseline. • Current-task VoI (public) : a current-task rule using the same public finite belief over unknown preference states as APA, with the same solver, cost/risk coefficients and positive-score selection. It has no access to future tasks. • Next-Task Only : public-belief value for the actual next task instance, without hidden answers; this is privileged lookahead. • Oracle Future-VoI : uses exact chronological subset dynamic programming to jointly optimize acquisitions and their timing, maximizing NU at the evaluation prices under the budget, with access to hidden answers and the actual future task sequence. It is a privileged reference, not a practical competing method; oracle regret is measured relative to it. Its dynamic program and tie-breaking are specified in Appendix B . • Oracle Future-VoI (unlimited) : Oracle Future-VoI without a budget limit. • Cost-matched heuristics. Random- k k , Frequency, Impact-only and LLM-Importance are all rerun under each user’s realized APA acquisition budget, C baseline , u total ≤ C APA , u total C^{\text{total}}_{\text{baseline},u}\leq C^{\text{total}}_{\text{APA },u} , in addition to the per-interaction cap B B . This separates acquisition quality from resource use. We compare APA with current-task VoI not because the two solve identical decisions, but because current-task VoI represents the natural wait-until-needed strategy. The comparison tests whether prospective acquisition provides value beyond deferring every question until it affects the current task. This comparison evaluates cross-task against current-task valuation under their respective acquisition protocols, including APA’s additional pre-sequence opportunity; it does not separately identify the effect of acquisition timing. Every policy is run with the same per-interaction budget B B , except Ask-Everything and Oracle Future-VoI (unlimited). The cap resets at each arrival. Prospective policies also receive one pre-sequence opportunity with no current task; current-task policies do not. Pareto sweeps vary B B and λ \lambda for every policy.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: Benefit is measured as cumulative task utility , CTU = ∑ t U ⁡ ( τ t ) \text{CTU}=\sum_{t}U(\tau_{t}) . Cost is measured as acquisition cost AC = ∑ C ask =\sum C_{\text{ask}} and risk cost RC = ∑ C risk =\sum C_{\text{risk}} ; we also report the raw number of questions. Our primary metric is net utility , NU = CTU − λ ​ AC − β ​ RC =\text{CTU}-\lambda\,\text{AC}-\beta\,\text{RC} . We further report: utility per question relative to Ask-Nothing; oracle regret ( NU oracle − NU \text{NU}_{\text{oracle}}-\text{NU} ); unnecessary query rate , the fraction of asked attributes with zero realized utility within the horizon; missed valuable rate ; gap precision and recall; and the rank agreement between predicted and oracle value (NDCG ( Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2002 ) and Spearman correlation).

sections.heading: Statistics.
sections.text: The resampling unit is a user’s task sequence. We report means with 95% pointwise percentile bootstrap confidence intervals ( Efron and Tibshirani, 1994 ) and use two-sided centered paired bootstrap tests (2,000 resamples, plus-one correction) with Holm correction within separate families: the 15 main-comparison contrasts (five comparators on IID, unseen and Overall), the four cost-matched contrasts, the two amortization-cohort contrasts, the 15 ablation contrasts, the 15 horizon contrasts, and the three endpoint-growth tests (Table 9 ).

sections.heading: Implementation.
sections.text: All LLM roles use Qwen3-8B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , temperature 0 and thinking disabled, for candidate recognition, forecasting and LLM baselines. Value integration and task solving are deterministic. The exact prompts are listed in Appendix D . Up to K = 10 K=10 fresh candidates are proposed per opportunity; recognized pending candidates are retained separately. All model outputs are cached, and every table and figure is generated from the logged results. Defaults are B = 0.5 B=0.5 , λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 , β = 0.25 \beta=0.25 , T = 10 T=10 , K = 10 K=10 . All reported Overall values pool IID and unseen users. A development-set comparison supports B = 0.5 B=0.5 : lowering it from 1 to 0.5 changes CTU by − 0.007 -0.007 , increases NU by 0.034 and reduces oracle regret ( B = 1 B=1 : CTU 7.074, NU 6.681, regret 0.336; B = 0.5 B=0.5 : CTU 7.067, NU 6.715, regret 0.298, over 90 development users); test results at B = 1 B=1 are reported in Appendix C .

sections.heading: Unseen preference combinations and parameter sensitivity.
sections.text: APA’s NU gain over Ask-Nothing is 0.400 on IID users and 0.531 on users with unseen preference combinations; split-specific main results are in Appendix G , Tables 12 and 13 . Overall coefficient/budget sensitivity is shown in Figure 7 .

sections.heading: Case studies.
sections.text: As an illustrative mechanism, seat preference can be valued before a later flight even while the current context concerns a hotel. A favorite color distractor has no task-utility terms and therefore has zero prospective gain.

sections.heading: Simulated users.
sections.text: ActiveWebPref uses synthetic profiles and a simulated user, which makes exact utilities and controlled ablations possible but cannot fully reflect real user behavior. Real users may answer vaguely, change their minds, or find questions annoying in ways that our cost model only approximates; the validity requirements and limitations of LLM-based user simulators are discussed in ( Balog and Zhai, 2025 ) . No completed blinded human evaluation, paraphrase/noise robustness study, or live-Web deployment is reported. The deterministic simulator binds structured attribute IDs to text; this does not validate how a real user understands a generated question.

sections.heading: Single backbone and benchmark.
sections.text: All LLM roles use Qwen3-8B, and all results come from one controlled benchmark; whether the findings hold with stronger backbones, other solvers, or other task distributions remains to be tested. APA also relies on a public schema for each task family to generate prototypes, so extending it to unseen task families would require inferring such schemas, for example with the LLM backbone.

sections.heading: Limited evidence for learned future-task weights.
sections.text: Replacing P ^ ​ ( f ∣ H t ) \hat{P}(f\mid H_{t}) with a uniform prior changes NU from 6.755 to 6.760 (Table 5 ); the paired contrast is not significant after Holm correction. Restricting value estimation to the actual next task lowers mean NU by 0.072; this contrast is also not significant after correction. Two possible explanations remain untested. First, the benchmark's regular task-family design may make a uniform distribution a strong approximation, leaving little room for the learned forecast to improve selection. Second, Qwen3-8B's limited capacity may constrain prediction quality. The current forecast uses prompting alone, without dedicated training, calibration, or a theoretical accuracy guarantee. Its reliability and the design of future-task-weight prediction therefore need further investigation.

sections.heading: Per-interaction budget.
sections.text: Under B = 0.5 B=0.5 , attributes whose asking cost exceeds the per-interaction budget cannot be asked by a budgeted policy, even when their cumulative value would justify the cost; at T = 20 T=20 this excludes 26 otherwise amortization-dependent pairs. A budget that accumulates across interactions would admit them.

sections.heading: Misspecified futures and drifting preferences.
sections.text: PPV depends on the estimated distribution of future tasks. If that estimate is wrong, the agent asks about preferences that are never used. Acquired preferences may also become stale, and combining APA with preference-update methods ( Sun et al., 2026 ) is a natural extension.

sections.heading: Privacy and consent.
sections.text: An agent that asks questions proactively could be misused to collect more personal data than needed. LLMs and LLM agents already leak private information in contexts where disclosure is inappropriate ( Mireshghallah et al., 2024 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) , and data minimization, giving an agent access only to the data a task needs, has been proposed as a defense ( Bagdasarian et al., 2024 ) . APA is designed to limit such over-collection. Its goal is selective acquisition, not maximal profile completion. Privacy risk is a modeled cost term, not a calibrated privacy guarantee. The simulator refuses all high-sensitivity requests and charges asking cost even on refusal. Practical policies can still attempt intrusive questions before learning a refusal; the implemented rule does not enforce an exception for task-required sensitive disclosure. In deployment, acquired attributes should be visible to users, editable, and deletable, and asking should require consent. All data in ActiveWebPref is synthetic and contains no real personal information.

sections.heading: 9. Conclusion
sections.text: The passive personalization and memory methods discussed here use only the preferences that users happen to reveal. We argued that long-term Web agents should selectively acquire missing user information when expected reuse justifies its cost. We formalized this as Active Preference Acquisition, defined Prospective Personalization Value over future tasks as a complement to current-task clarification, and characterized an amortization regime that current-task valuation systematically misses because no single use justifies the cost of asking. In controlled long-term personalization tasks, our experiments support the reuse-based motivation: at T = 20 T=20 , amortization-dependent preferences make up 34.4% of budget-feasible valuable initially missing preferences, and APA acquires 80.3% of them while Current-task VoI (public) acquires 10 of 198; under matched asking-cost caps, APA selects better questions than heuristic baselines; cross-task, cost-aware acquisition recovers most of exhaustive asking’s utility gain with far fewer questions, and its mean advantage is larger at T = 20 T=20 than at T = 1 T=1 . Future work should test the effect under richer task distributions and with real users. A personalized agent should learn not everything about a user, but the things whose reuse makes them worth asking about.

An unknown categorical attribute takes every legal value; an unknown scalar takes its lower bound, integer midpoint and upper bound; an unknown price range within [ minimum , ceiling ] [\text{minimum},\text{ceiling}] takes the proportions ( 0 , 0.4 ) (0,0.4) , ( 0.3 , 0.6 ) (0.3,0.6) and ( 0.6 , 0.9 ) (0.6,0.9) , and a known range raises the lower bound of an unknown ceiling. sections.heading: Oracle Future-VoI.
sections.text: The oracle solves a dynamic program over T + 1 T+1 decision nodes: the pre-sequence opportunity, which yields no utility, and the arrival of each task; the value after the last node is zero. The state is the node and the set M M of attributes acquired so far; an action asks any subset S S of unacquired attributes with ∑ m ∈ S c m ≤ B \sum_{m\in S}c_{m}\leq B . Because the budget resets at every node, no remaining-budget dimension is needed. Values use hidden answers, the actual future tasks, the shared solver and NU at the evaluation prices. Candidates exclude known, non-queryable and high-sensitivity attributes, attributes with c m > B c_{m}>B , and attributes no task in the sequence uses, leaving 4–12 attributes per user at B = 0.5 B=0.5 . All feasible subsets at every node are enumerated with memoization and no pruning, so the solution is exact for this candidate pool; the largest number of cached states is 36,404 over all users at T = 10 T=10 and 77,364 over the amortization cohort at T = 20 T=20 (bound ( T + 2 ) ​ 2 n (T+2)\,2^{n} for n n candidates). Values within 10 − 12 10^{-12} are tied and broken by the smallest cumulative asking cost so far, then the fewest acquisitions, then the bitmask, which favors deferring an acquisition when deferral loses nothing. The 0% before-use rate in Table 3 therefore shows that an NU-optimal schedule within this candidate pool never needs to acquire these attributes before first use, not that waiting is strictly better. Asking earlier can be strictly better when the budget binds: the logs contain two such early acquisitions at T = 10 T=10 (all users) and two at T = 20 T=20 (amortization cohort), none of a designated attribute. For example, a restaurant-radius question (cost 0.2) and a meal-budget question (cost 0.4) do not fit together within B = 0.5 B=0.5 at the task that uses both, so the radius is acquired one task earlier.

sections.text: Random- k k shuffles the remaining candidates with one of five fixed seeds at each opportunity; Frequency ranks by the estimated reuse ∑ f n ^ f ​ R ​ ( m , f ) \sum_{f}\hat{n}_{f}R(m,f) of § 4.2 ; Impact-only ranks by max f ⁡ I ⁡ ( m , f ) \max_{f}I(m,f) , recomputed after each answer, with ties broken by attribute ID; LLM-Importance keeps the backbone’s ranking within an opportunity. None applies a positive-value threshold: each asks candidates in rank order, skipping any that does not fit and continuing with later ones, under the smaller of the remaining per-interaction budget and the user’s remaining total cap, which is set to APA’s realized total asking cost; refused questions also consume the cap. The caps bound expenditure but do not equalize it.

sections.heading: Missed valuable rate.
sections.text: An initially missing preference m m of user u u is valuable if adding its true answer alone to P 0 P_{0} raises realized CTU over the user’s T T tasks by more than its weighted cost λ ​ c m + β ​ C risk ​ ( m ) \lambda c_{m}+\beta C_{\text{risk}}(m) plus a fixed margin of 0.2, so that only preferences with a clear net gain, not any positive gain, count as valuable. The margin is a descriptive threshold that was never tuned; it affects only which preferences MVMR counts, not any acquisition decision. Unlike the diagnostic of § 6.2 , this uses realized rather than public-belief gains and does not filter by B B . MVMR u is the fraction of u u ’s valuable preferences that the policy did not acquire; it is averaged over users with at least one valuable preference (49 at T = 10 T=10 and 102 at T = 20 T=20 in the amortization cohorts), and undefined for the others.

sections.text: English translations of the system instructions and user-message templates used in the experiments are given below; the original instructions were in Chinese. sections.heading: Gap proposer (Module A).
sections.text: System message. You are responsible for discovering user preferences that are not yet known and can be reused in later tasks. Do not extract facts that have already been stated. Known attributes are determined by memory/history.observed_attributes and publicly declared exact aliases. Only the following public groups declare exact aliases: <public_alias_groups>. Different groups are not guaranteed to have the same value and cannot be inferred from one another. history.past_task_families records only past task categories; it never means that preferences for those categories have been stated. A null current_task means that the task sequence has not started and there is no current task: identify missing preferences useful for future tasks using only visible history and memory; do not invent a current task or domain. Attribute IDs whose values are known or that this user has refused to answer are <known_or_blocked_ids>; do not output these IDs. Candidate IDs already identified but not yet answered are <pending_ids>; their values remain unknown and the controller will continue to re-evaluate them, so do not propose them again. queryability_observed describes only the current user; a missing entry means unknown and permits asking. Do not assume that this user has refused an attribute because another user refused it or because the field is privacy-sensitive. Select <target> unstated attributes from the complete attribute_catalogue. Prioritize preferences that can be reused over the long term or within an explicitly defined planning window and may improve tasks; a stability label alone does not imply future value. Infer stability from public attribute descriptions and output stable/semi-stable/ephemeral; no gold labels are provided. Use visible history to judge which preferences are worth learning for later use, without guessing attribute values. Visible historical task counts are <visible_history_family_counts>; prioritize unknown, reusable preferences needed by repeatedly occurring categories, without treating the occurrence of a task as evidence that its preferences are known. Do not prioritize ephemeral small-talk fields when other reusable unknown preferences remain. Do not substitute catalogue display order for a value judgment. Generate a natural-language question for each attribute that asks only about that attribute; do not say that the user has already mentioned its unknown value. Each question must match the field’s allowed_values or value_schema. Do not mix numerical values with different units or scopes; preserve the ranges and windows defined by canonical_question. Return only JSON {"candidates":{"<attribute_id>":{"stability":"...","question":"..."},...}}. candidates must be a dictionary of exactly <target> distinct unknown attributes, keyed by attribute ID, with only stability/question in each value; do not use an array or an attribute_id subfield, and do not repeat keys. Stability and future usefulness are independent concepts; even a stable small-talk preference may yield no task benefit. A hard numerical budget ceiling and an ideal range are different information and must not be treated as exact aliases. value_schema and canonical_question define the currency, units, scope, and questioning window; preserve these semantics and ask about only the corresponding attribute. When selecting candidates, first check unknown constraints that determine feasibility in repeatedly occurring historical contexts, then consider soft preferences that can change the chosen option. A hard resource limit can be reused within a planning window even if it remains fixed only within that window; do not rank it below small-talk fields for that reason. Hard ceilings and ideal ranges play different roles; an unknown one cannot automatically be treated as known from the other. stable denotes a usual long-term tendency, semi-stable denotes a preference that may change with resources or planning context, and ephemeral denotes a one-time intention. A validity window specifies only when a value applies and does not automatically determine stability; being privacy-sensitive or unqueryable does not imply ephemeral. No gold stability labels are provided; infer them from public descriptions. When a current task is present, replace the null-task sentence with: The current_task can already be completed; still identify missing preferences useful for future tasks. Web agents increasingly serve the same user across repeated online tasks such as booking travel, shopping, and scheduling, so their long-term usefulness depends on how well they know the user’s preferences. Passive memory and personalization methods cannot obtain preferences the user never reveals, and clarification methods that value a question by its benefit to the current task overlook the benefit of reusing the answer in later tasks. We study Active Preference Acquisition (APA): which missing preferences are worth the cost of asking? We define the Prospective Personalization Value (PPV) of a missing preference as its expected cumulative utility gain over future tasks minus the effort and disclosure-risk cost of asking, and select questions under a per-interaction budget. We characterize when cumulative reuse justifies acquisition despite insufficient single-task benefit, and evaluate this regime with an initial-profile diagnostic. APA computes the counterfactual gain of each candidate preference on public task prototypes with the agent’s own task solver and aggregates it by the expected reuse of each task family. We evaluate it on ActiveWebPref, a controlled longitudinal benchmark with hidden but queryable user profiles and exact task utilities. At a horizon of 20 tasks, 34.4% of budget-feasible valuable missing preferences are amortization-dependent; APA acquires 80.3% of them, whereas current-task value of information acquires 5.1%. Under per-user asking-cost caps matched to APA’s realized expenditure, APA achieves higher net utility than random, frequency-based, impact-based and LLM-ranked selection. In our cost setting, asking about every unknown preference yields lower net utility than not asking, while APA recovers 84.2% of its utility gain with 27.6% of its questions. The value of acquiring a user preference should account for its reuse across future tasks, not only its benefit to the task at hand. Keywords: Personalized Web agents, user modeling, preference elicitation, value of information, long-term memory 1. Introduction Web agents can now carry out realistic Web tasks such as online shopping and navigating real-world websites ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Deng et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) , and they are moving from one-shot assistance to persistent service. The same agent may book a user’s conference travel in March, order office supplies in April, and reserve a team dinner in May. Its usefulness over time then depends less on any single task than on how well it knows the user : that the user avoids red-eye flights, keeps hotels under a per-night budget, and needs vegetarian options. This paper studies that user-modeling problem for users of persistent Web agents: which missing preferences a persistent Web agent should acquire, and when doing so pays off. Valuable preferences, however, need not appear in the interaction history. Personalization methods condition on past behavior ( Salemi et al., 2024 ) or infer profiles from what users have said ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and long-term memory systems decide how to extract, store, retrieve, and update observed information ( Packer et al., 2023 ; Zhong et al., 2024 ; Chhikara et al., 2025 ; Rasmussen et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . These methods work with evidence that exists; a preference the user has never had reason to mention or to reveal through behavior cannot be extracted or retrieved. Asking can fill such gaps, but asking is not free: each question costs the user effort, and each answer discloses personal information. An agent therefore cannot simply ask about everything; in our experiments, asking about every unknown preference, or about whatever an LLM deems most worth knowing, yields lower net utility than not asking at all (§ 6 ). Figure 1. A preference that is useless now can be valuable later. In session t t the user asks for a hotel, and the seat preference m m is unknown. For the current task, knowing m m has no value ( V current ​ ( m ) ≈ 0 V_{\text{current}}(m)\approx 0 ), so a clarification agent does not ask. Every later seat selection needs it, so V future ​ ( m ) > 0 V_{\text{future}}(m)>0 ; when this expected cumulative benefit exceeds the one-time cost of asking, acquiring it once and reusing it is worthwhile. Timeline from session t to t+3. In session t the user books a hotel; a missing seat preference has no immediate value. In sessions t+1 to t+3 flight, conference-travel and business-trip bookings each require selecting a seat, so acquiring the preference once and reusing it is valuable. Valuing each question by the current task does not resolve this either. Current-task clarification and value-of-information (VoI) methods ask when a question improves the current task enough to justify its cost ( Rao and Daumé III, 2018 ; Aliannejadi et al., 2019 ; Zamani et al., 2020 ; Dong et al., 2026 ) . While booking a hotel, the agent can finish without the user’s seat preference, so current-task VoI does not ask (Figure 1 ). Why not wait and ask when a flight is booked? Because even then, a single booking’s gain may not cover the cost of asking; only reuse across many later bookings does. A criterion that values a question only by the task at hand then never acquires such a preference, however often it is reused (Proposition 3.1 ). An agent therefore needs to value acquisition across tasks: Which currently unknown user preferences are worth acquiring, because their benefit across future tasks outweighs the cost of asking? We call this problem Active Preference Acquisition (APA). At each interaction the agent holds a partial profile and can already complete the current task; it decides which missing preferences to ask about and stores the answers persistently. Unlike cold-start elicitation or within-session clarification, APA interleaves acquisition with ongoing service and values persistent attributes by their reuse across heterogeneous future tasks. We define the Prospective Personalization Value (PPV) of a missing preference: its expected utility gain across future tasks, minus the effort and disclosure-risk cost of asking. PPV complements clarification rather than generalizing it, and the key distinction is in how a preference is valued, not when it is asked: a cross-task criterion may still ask at the first relevant task. We estimate PPV by counterfactual reuse valuation . For each candidate missing preference, the agent’s own task solver computes how much knowing it would change utility on public task prototypes, and these gains are aggregated by the expected reuse of each task family; questions are then selected under asking cost, disclosure risk and a per-interaction budget. To test when this helps and by how much, we build ActiveWebPref, a controlled longitudinal testbed modeled on personalized Web services, with hidden but queryable user profiles, multi-domain task sequences, and exact task utilities. It isolates the value of preference acquisition, which existing memory benchmarks do not measure ( Wu et al., 2025a ; Maharana et al., 2024 ) , and does not evaluate agents acting on live websites. Contributions. (1) Problem. We formulate Active Preference Acquisition and define PPV. We show that a criterion valuing only the current task never acquires a preference whose benefit on every single task is below the asking cost, however often it is reused, whereas PPV assigns it positive value once cumulative reuse covers that cost (Proposition 3.1 ). (2) Method. APA estimates PPV by counterfactual reuse valuation: the agent’s own task solver computes each candidate’s gain on public task prototypes, weighted by the expected reuse of each task family, and an adaptive greedy policy selects questions under asking cost, disclosure risk and a per-interaction budget (§ 4 ). (3) Benchmark. ActiveWebPref is a controlled longitudinal benchmark with 16 task families, hidden but queryable user profiles and exact task utilities, so the counterfactual value of an unasked preference can be measured; an initial-profile diagnostic identifies amortization-dependent preferences (§ 5 ). Code, data and prompts are available at https://github.com/xiaoqi-7/Active-Preference-Acquisition . (4) Findings. At a horizon of T = 20 T=20 tasks, 34.4% of budget-feasible valuable initially missing preferences are amortization-dependent; APA acquires 80.3% of them and Current-task VoI (public) 5.1%, while the NU-maximizing oracle acquires 44.9%, so the aim is selective rather than maximal acquisition. Among users with at least one such preference, APA improves whole-sequence net utility over Current-task VoI (public) at T = 20 T=20 (Holm p = 0.021 p=0.021 ) but not significantly at T = 10 T=10 . Under per-user asking-cost caps matched to APA’s realized expenditure, APA achieves higher net utility than random, frequency-based, impact-based and LLM-ranked selection (all Holm p ≤ 0.0025 p\leq 0.0025 ). In our cost setting, cost-blind asking yields lower net utility than not asking, while APA recovers 84.2% of exhaustive asking’s utility gain with 27.6% of its questions (§ 6 ). 2. Related Work User modeling and personalization. Personalized systems condition generation or ranking on user profiles, given as explicit persona statements ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) or drawn from behavioral history ( Salemi et al., 2024 ) . Recent LLM agents continuously infer and refine a unified user profile from dialogue turns ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , or update preference memories as user behavior evolves by fusing short- and long-term averages ( Sun et al., 2026 ) . These methods infer preferences from evidence that already exists. They cannot recover a preference that has never been expressed or revealed through behavior, and they do not decide which unobserved preferences are worth eliciting for future tasks. Preference elicitation. Decision-theoretic preference elicitation frames question asking as a POMDP that trades question cost against the quality of a final decision ( Boutilier, 2002 ) . Recommender systems ask new users to rate items in a cold-start interview ( Rashid et al., 2002 ) , possibly adapting the next item to earlier answers with a decision tree ( Golbandi et al., 2011 ) , and use active learning in collaborative filtering more broadly ( Elahi et al., 2016 ) . Conversational recommenders decide within a session which item or attribute to ask about next ( Christakopoulou et al., 2016 ; Sun and Zhang, 2018 ; Lei et al., 2020a ; Lei et al., 2020b ; Deng et al., 2021 ; Jannach et al., 2021 ) . LLMs have also been used to elicit preferences through open-ended questions: GATE prompts models to elicit a user’s intended task behavior ( Li et al., 2025 ) , and STaR-GATE fine-tunes a questioner to ask useful clarifying questions ( Andukuri et al., 2024 ) . APA differs from this work in three ways. (i) When and why to ask. Conversational elicitation asks in order to finish the current session. Cold-start interviews do ask for future benefit, but in a single onboarding step before any task is served. In APA, questions are interleaved with ongoing tasks that can already be completed, and each question is justified by its expected effect on future tasks. (ii) Scope. Elicitation targets item ratings or attributes within a single catalog. APA acquires persistent user attributes that are reused across heterogeneous task families, such as flights, hotels, dining, and scheduling. (iii) Valuation target. Like prior elicitation, APA weighs benefit against the cost of asking; the difference is that the benefit is counted across the heterogeneous future tasks that reuse the answer, rather than within one decision or session. APA builds on established value-of-information and preference-elicitation principles ( Howard, 1966 ; Boutilier, 2002 ) , operationalizing them for persistent preferences reused across heterogeneous tasks, and adds a benchmark in which the counterfactual value of an unasked preference can be measured. Long-term memory for agents. Surveys organize agent memory by its sources, forms, and operations (writing, management, and reading) ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) . Memory architectures give LLM agents persistent state through hierarchical context management ( Packer et al., 2023 ) , memory streams with reflection ( Park et al., 2023 ) , forgetting-aware stores ( Zhong et al., 2024 ) , scalable extraction and retrieval ( Chhikara et al., 2025 ) , and temporal knowledge graphs ( Rasmussen et al., 2025 ) . ProMem improves memory extraction itself: it extracts details, events, and relations separately, checks completeness to recover missed events, and verifies atomic facts ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . Benchmarks such as LongMemEval ( Wu et al., 2025a ) and LoCoMo ( Maharana et al., 2024 ) test whether facts present in the history can be recalled. PrefEval tests whether models follow stated or implicit preferences ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) , and PersonaMem whether they track preferences that evolve across sessions ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) ; both find that preferences already expressed are often not followed. These systems answer how to retain and use what is known . APA addresses which unknown information should be learned , and can run on top of any of them. Clarification and value of information. Asking clarifying questions has been studied in information retrieval ( Aliannejadi et al., 2019 ; Zamani et al., 2020 ) and in NLP, for example by ranking questions by expected value of perfect information ( Rao and Daumé III, 2018 ) . For LLM agents, the IN3 benchmark annotates which details of a vague task are missing, and Mistral-Interact is trained to ask about them before executing ( Qian et al., 2024 ) , and Ask-before-Plan studies clarification before travel planning ( Zhang et al., 2024b ) . Proactive Agent instead anticipates and offers help that the user has not requested ( Lu et al., 2025 ) . Dong et al. ( Dong et al., 2026 ) formalize when an agent should ask rather than act by weighing the expected utility gain of a question on the current decision against the cost it imposes on the user. Two lines of work look beyond the current response: one labels response preferences by simulating future conversation turns, teaching models when to ask clarifying questions ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) , and CollabLLM trains models with a multiturn-aware reward estimated from simulated future conversations ( Wu et al., 2025b ) . Their horizon, however, is later turns of the same conversation, whereas the horizon of APA is future tasks across sessions. Abstracting from these methods, current-task clarification scores a question about m m as V cur ​ ( m ) = Δ ​ U ​ ( τ t , m ) − C ⁡ ( m ) , V_{\text{cur}}(m)=\Delta U(\tau_{t};m)-C(m), whereas APA scores the same preference by its value over the tasks that follow, P ​ P ​ V T ​ ( m ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ ∑ k = t + 1 T Δ ​ U ​ ( τ k , m ) ] − C ⁡ ( m ) . PPV_{T}(m)=\mathbb{E}\Big[\textstyle\sum_{k=t+1}^{T}\Delta U(\tau_{k};m)\Big]-C(m). The two scores answer different questions and are complementary. Howard’s formulation values information for a single decision problem ( Howard, 1966 ) , and the non-myopic VoI of Krause and Guestrin ( Krause and Guestrin, 2005 ) selects a budget-constrained set of observations jointly, rather than greedily, to reduce uncertainty in one fixed model. These principles can accommodate long-term benefit; APA instantiates them as a longitudinal personalization decision. The information is stored, and it pays off across many future tasks drawn from an uncertain task distribution. Web agents. Benchmarks for Web agents such as WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , Mind2Web ( Deng et al., 2023 ) , and WebArena ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) pose each episode as a single, self-contained instruction, with no user state carried across tasks. Personalized Web agents have recently been studied through PersonalWAB, which pairs simulated users’ profiles and behavior histories with personalized search, recommendation, and review tasks and whose multi-turn track lets the agent clarify a request with a simulated user ( Cai et al., 2025 ) , and Persona2Web, which requires agents on the open Web to resolve ambiguous queries from long user histories ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . Both personalize mainly from histories, and any questions serve the current request. Neither studies which missing preferences an agent should acquire for future tasks. 3. The APA Framework APA estimates the terms of Eq. ( 1 ) with four modules (Figure 2 ). Its core is counterfactual reuse valuation (§ 4.3 ) combined with cost-sensitive budgeted selection (§ 4.4 ); gap discovery (§ 4.1 ) and future reuse modeling (§ 4.2 ) are implementation components that supply candidates and reuse estimates. To isolate the acquisition decision, all LLM roles share the same backbone, and all policies share the same deterministic task solver. Prompts are given in Appendix D . 4.1. Preference Gap Discovery The agent knows a complete public attribute catalogue but not the user's missing values; it selects which unknown fields to evaluate for acquisition. Given ( H t , P t ) (H_{t},P_{t}) and the arrived task (null before the sequence), a proposer LLM selects min ⁡ ( K , | 𝒜 t | ) \min(K,|\mathcal{A}_{t}|) distinct IDs from the allowed unknown-field set 𝒜 t \mathcal{A}_{t} , predicting stability and a natural-language question q i q_{i} . The catalogue supplies each description, so the resulting candidates retain the form ( m i , description i , stability i , q i ) (m_{i},\text{description}_{i},\text{stability}_{i},q_{i}) . ActiveWebPref and Experimental Setup Existing long-term memory benchmarks either place the information needed for each question in the history or ask models to abstain when it is absent ( Wu et al., 2025a ; Maharana et al., 2024 ) ; none rewards acquiring missing information. APA instead requires preferences that are useful but initially absent from the history . It also requires task utilities that can be computed exactly, so that the benefit of a question can be measured without an LLM judge. We therefore build ActiveWebPref as a controlled longitudinal testbed. The benchmarks discussed in § 2 do not directly provide a protocol with hidden but queryable profiles and counterfactual utilities of unasked preferences. ActiveWebPref is deliberately controlled so that the counterfactual utility of an unasked preference is known exactly, allowing us to measure whether each question was worth asking. This control comes at the cost of realism, which we discuss in § 8 . 5.1. Benchmark Construction Domains and task families. ActiveWebPref covers five service domains: Travel (flight booking, hotel selection, ground transport, conference trips), Dining (restaurant choice, reservation, takeaway), Shopping (product selection, gifts, repeat purchases), Scheduling (meetings, recurring events, appointments), and Work/Conference (conference, coordination, work events): 16 task families in total. Task options are synthetic structured alternatives, rather than items taken from live Web catalogues. Hidden user profiles. Each synthetic user has 27 attributes. Each attribute has a ground-truth value and the following metadata: • stability : stable, semi-stable, or ephemeral; • sensitivity : low, medium, or high; • a normalized fixed asking cost c m ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] c_{m}\in[0,1] ; • the set of relevant task families ℛ ⁡ ( m ) \mathcal{R}(m) and an impact level; • whether it is initially observed; • whether it is queryable. Between 40% and 60% of useful attributes are hidden at t = 0 t=0 . Profiles are stored separately from dialogues and are visible only to the user simulator and the evaluator. The privileged oracle also accesses the hidden profile; practical policies receive the public catalogue and visible profile/history only. Task sequences. For each user we save a separate initial context and 20 future tasks. Main CTU evaluates the first T = 10 T=10 future tasks; horizon scaling uses nested prefixes T ∈ { 1 , 3 , 5 , 10 , 20 } T\in\{1,3,5,10,20\} . The generator varies reuse frequency, cross-domain relevance, acquisition cost, sensitivity, and attribute dependence, to evaluate their effects on acquisition decisions. It includes five kinds of attributes: • attributes with heterogeneous reuse: some are used once, some repeatedly, some never; • cross-domain attributes (e.g., meeting mode) as well as domain-specific ones (e.g., seat preference); • distractors : attributes that look personal but never affect utility; • attributes that are high-value but also high-cost or high-sensitivity; • correlated attributes, whose joint value may be less than the sum of their individual values. Exact utilities and user simulator. As in evaluations that separate user-side private information from the agent ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Balog and Zhai, 2025 ) , each task has a candidate set, for example flight options with seat, layover, and price attributes. The solver picks the best candidate under the agent’s current profile, and utility is the score of that pick under P u ∗ P^{*}_{u} . The simulator answers only questions that map to a single queryable attribute and never reveals other attributes. Requests for non-queryable or high-sensitivity fields are refused, and the refused question still incurs its asking cost. Risk is charged only on successful disclosure. The main experiments use a deterministic structured answer mode. Splits. The two disjoint test splits contain IID users and users with unseen preference combinations. All splits were frozen before any test-set evaluation. The train split is not used by any policy, for parameter selection, or for prototype sampling; it is retained as a benchmark split and used to verify that the unseen combinations occur in neither train nor dev. ActiveWebPref uses synthetic profiles and a simulated user, which makes exact utilities and controlled ablations possible but cannot fully reflect real user behavior. Real users may answer vaguely, change their minds, or find questions annoying in ways that our cost model only approximates; the validity requirements and limitations of LLM-based user simulators are discussed in ( Balog and Zhai, 2025 ) . No completed blinded human evaluation, paraphrase/noise robustness study, or live-Web deployment is reported. The deterministic simulator binds structured attribute IDs to text; this does not validate how a real user understands a generated question. Single backbone and benchmark. All LLM roles use Qwen3-8B, and all results come from one controlled benchmark; whether the findings hold with stronger backbones, other solvers, or other task distributions remains to be tested. APA also relies on a public schema for each task family to generate prototypes, so extending it to unseen task families would require inferring such schemas, for example with the LLM backbone. Limited evidence for learned future-task weights. Replacing P ^ ​ ( f ∣ H t ) \hat{P}(f\mid H_{t}) with a uniform prior changes NU from 6.755 to 6.760 (Table 5 ); the paired contrast is not significant after Holm correction. Restricting value estimation to the actual next task lowers mean NU by 0.072; this contrast is also not significant after correction. Two possible explanations remain untested. First, the benchmark's regular task-family design may make a uniform distribution a strong approximation, leaving little room for the learned forecast to improve selection. Second, Qwen3-8B's limited capacity may constrain prediction quality. The current forecast uses prompting alone, without dedicated training, calibration, or a theoretical accuracy guarantee. Its reliability and the design of future-task-weight prediction therefore need further investigation. Per-interaction budget. Under B = 0.5 B=0.5 , attributes whose asking cost exceeds the per-interaction budget cannot be asked by a budgeted policy, even when their cumulative value would justify the cost; at T = 20 T=20 this excludes 26 otherwise amortization-dependent pairs. A budget that accumulates across interactions would admit them. Misspecified futures and drifting preferences. PPV depends on the estimated distribution of future tasks. If that estimate is wrong, the agent asks about preferences that are never used. Acquired preferences may also become stale, and combining APA with preference-update methods ( Sun et al., 2026 ) is a natural extension. Privacy and consent. An agent that asks questions proactively could be misused to collect more personal data than needed. LLMs and LLM agents already leak private information in contexts where disclosure is inappropriate ( Mireshghallah et al., 2024 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) , and data minimization, giving an agent access only to the data a task needs, has been proposed as a defense ( Bagdasarian et al., 2024 ) . APA is designed to limit such over-collection. Its goal is selective acquisition, not maximal profile completion. Privacy risk is a modeled cost term, not a calibrated privacy guarantee. The simulator refuses all high-sensitivity requests and charges asking cost even on refusal. Practical policies can still attempt intrusive questions before learning a refusal; the implemented rule does not enforce an exception for task-required sensitive disclosure. In deployment, acquired attributes should be visible to users, editable, and deletable, and asking should require consent. All data in ActiveWebPref is synthetic and contains no real personal information. 9. Conclusion The passive personalization and memory methods discussed here use only the preferences that users happen to reveal. We argued that long-term Web agents should selectively acquire missing user information when expected reuse justifies its cost. We formalized this as Active Preference Acquisition, defined Prospective Personalization Value over future tasks as a complement to current-task clarification, and characterized an amortization regime that current-task valuation systematically misses because no single use justifies the cost of asking. In controlled long-term personalization tasks, our experiments support the reuse-based motivation: at T = 20 T=20 , amortization-dependent preferences make up 34.4% of budget-feasible valuable initially missing preferences, and APA acquires 80.3% of them while Current-task VoI (public) acquires 10 of 198; under matched asking-cost caps, APA selects better questions than heuristic baselines; cross-task, cost-aware acquisition recovers most of exhaustive asking’s utility gain with far fewer questions, and its mean advantage is larger at T = 20 T=20 than at T = 1 T=1 . Future work should test the effect under richer task distributions and with real users. A personalized agent should learn not everything about a user, but the things whose reuse makes them worth asking about. References Aliannejadi et al. (2019) M. Aliannejadi, H. Zamani, F.
